Topic:Mining and Metals Industry

Liberty Bell Bay is the only manganese alloy smelter in Australia. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

The future of mothballed Tasmanian manganese smelter Liberty Bell Bay has been thrown into doubt again, after administrators confirmed Adroit Capital is no longer engaged in negotiations as the preferred bidder.

Late last month administrators EY Parthenon announced that the preferred bidder was a consortium made up of Adroit Capital, OM Holdings and White Oak.

Smelter workers have been told by the administrators that there is a Monday deadline to secure alternative funding for the site's continuation.

A member of the consortium designated as the preferred bidder for the Liberty Bell Bay manganese smelter has effectively pulled out, with workers told by administrators have until Monday to secure alternative funding.

Liberty Bell Bay, in northern Tasmania, was placed into administration in March, and late last month the administrators EY Parthenon announced the preferred bidder — a consortium including Perth-based Adroit Capital, ASX-listed OM Holdings and White Oak, a US private equity firm that was a secured lender to former parent Sanjeev Gupta's GFG Alliance.

A town hall meeting in George Town on Friday morning was attended by EY Parthenon administrator Morgan Kelly, Liberty Bell Bay workers and Federal Labor member for Bass, Jess Teesdale.

A consortium headed by Adroit Capital is announced as the preferred bidder for the smelter in northern Tasmania, as federal and state government pledge another $5 million to support workers in the weeks ahead.

Speaking on the condition of anonymity, one worker who was present told the ABC that Mr Kelly had told this morning's meeting that Adroit Capital had not been able to come up with their portion of the funding and had effectively "pulled out of the consortium".

"So, we've got another meeting lunchtime on Monday, and they'll be announcing then if they've got the funding and things are going ahead or if the [smelter] will be closing down."

Adroit Capital is no longer engaged in exclusive negotiations with the administrators of Liberty Bell Bay. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

The ABC understands government and consortium funding ran out on Thursday and EY Parthenon is now liable for payroll expenses of $145,000 a day.

The worker said Mr Kelly told workers that EY Parthenon was returning to the other parties who had expressed interest in taking over Liberty Bell Bay, to see whether they would join the consortium.

However, he said Mr Kelly was "very non-committal" about the prospect of further funding.

In a statement from EY on Friday morning, Mr Kelly said:

"We recognise this further uncertainty for employees, their families and the wider Bell Bay community is difficult, and we are working to provide clarity as quickly as possible."

EY Parthenon confirmed difficulties had arisen with "a number of critical financing, supplier and government arrangements".

Liberty Bell Bay smelter employs more than 200 workers. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

When the preferred consortium was announced in late May, the federal and state governments had contributed a further $5 million in public funding to secure the 216-strong workforce at Liberty Bell Bay, which has been under care and maintenance for more than a year.

Total government assistance since Liberty Bell Bay went into administration now totals $9.6 million.

In a statement, EY Parthenon said a condition of the funding was the consortium providing funding for non-workforce operating costs "to enable accelerated confirmatory due diligence and completion of the proposed acquisition".

"Urgent discussions are underway to secure further funding, to enable an alternate pathway to be pursued."

Australian Workers' Union Tasmanian assistant secretary Robert Flanagan said the likelihood of funding being secured would depend on "how things go over the next three days".

"It was clear that there was a lot of work the administrator had to do to try and find a way forward and that he would update us on Monday about how that was going," Mr Flanagan said.

Australian Workers' Union assistant secretary Robert Flanagan says the news that Adroit Capital is no longe a preferred bidder for Liberty Bell Bay is a shock for workers. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

He said it was unclear what had caused difficulties in the sale process, but workers were "very concerned" about whether or not a sale could be made.

"All that we know is that they were having difficulties finalising the sale process with Adroit and it seemed to be implicit that funding was a part of that," he said.

The ABC understands federal Labor member for Bass Jess Teesdale has said she was working to secure federal funding to cover the cost of worker's wages and keep the smelter open while a new buyer was secured.

Adroit Capital and White Oak have been approached for comment.

Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff told reporters in George Town that he was "extremely disappointed" by the news from Liberty Bell Bay's administrators.

Mr Rockliff insisted that due diligence had been done on the members of the consortium and said he had spoken with federal Industry Minister Tim Ayres on Thursday night in an effort to ensure workers would continue to be paid and to preserve the country's only manganese smelter at a time of rising global demand.

Liberty Bell Bay smelter has been in care and maintenance for over a year. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Tasmanian Resources Minister Felix Ellis declined to say whether any further state or federal assistance would be provided, or to confirm whether the $5 million extension announced in May — which has not been drawn down — would still be available.

Mr Ellis said the additional loan funding had been provided "on the basis that it helps as a bridge to a near-term sale, so the plant can get "up and running".

"Unfortunately that hasn't happened in this process," Mr Ellis said.

"We're working through due diligence over the course of the weekend and I understand the administrator is working hard for other potential purchases.

"It's too early to say at this stage although we welcome, if there are credible buyers with the capability to restart the facility and invest in its future, we welcome those people coming forward."

Federal Member for Bass Jess Teesdale said administrators EY Parthenon were "really open about where we're at, and what we're going to be working on over the weekend, to try and make sure that we get some good news on Monday."

But Mr Rockliff would not rule out the permanent closure of Liberty Bell Bay if negotiations over the weekend were not successful.

"We'll just have to take one step at a time, I'm not going to answer hypotheticals at this stage," he said.
